newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition to press for more reforms.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition to press for more reforms.

text.p: Serbian opposition leader Vuk Draskovic, ignoring government warnings to stop daily protests now that they have achieved their main aim, pledged to keep up pressure for democratic reforms in the country.
Draskovic, a co-leader of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition, told thousands of demonstrators on the 86th day of street protests that 1997 was a decisive year for Serbia.
"Serbia is in a hurry -- with the energy that we have fired up in the first half, the victory of freedom and democracy in the second half is certain," he told the cheering crowd in central Belgrade.

The rally took place despite warnings that the protests should stop now that the government has finally recognised opposition victories in local elections last November, the main demand of the demonstrators.

However, opposition leaders have pledged to continue the protests until opposition-led councils are operating in all 14 cities and towns involved, including Belgrade, which is expected to happen next week.

They have also made clear all along that they want further reforms from the authoritarian government led by Slobodan Milosevic, including an overhaul of the state-run media which he uses to help keep him in power.

"We are only nearing the end of the first half of our defence of the November 17 election results -- the second half of the struggle for democratic elections will happen before the end of the year," Draskovic said.
Earlier in the day the Belgrade city election commission removed the last legal obstacle to the opposition's assuming control over the city by verifying the mandates of the newly-elected deputies.
Some 7,000 teachers demonstrated in front of the Serbian parliament demanding higher wages and better school conditions, adding to the wave of protests that has rocked Serbia.
Earlier on Thursday, opposition leaders suggested that civil disobedience was one form of pressure and the Zajedno mayor of Kragujevac called on his citizens on Thursday to employ it.

"I invite the citizens of Kragujevac to citizens' disobedience. I call on them not to pay interest on the property tax but only the principal," the independent Belgrade newspaper Nasa Borba quoted Veroljub Stevanovic as saying.

Citizens of Kragujevac were served their property tax returns for 1996 and were due to pay interest rates standing at 200 or more dinars ($35), a large sum in a country where the average monthly wage stands at some $150.
He said the republican authorities owed Kragujevac citizens more than 24 million dinars ($4 million) alone in social security compensation, including child allowance, since last March.
Stevanovic's opposition authorities took charge of the city last month with limited powers and empty coffers to finance the city's decaying infrastructure.

"What we are in charge of is the waterworks, sewerage and garbage disposal. Our biggest problem is the economy which is under the complete control of republican bodies," Zoran Zivkovic, the Zajedno Mayor of the neighbouring town of Nis, told Reuters.
